clinicalPearls: CASPR2 antibodies produce a broad phenotype spanning central and peripheral nervous system, unlike the largely central picture of LGI1.
Morvan syndrome is the classic severe presentation, combining peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, dysautonomia, severe insomnia (agrypnia excitata) and encephalopathy.
Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability manifests as neuromyotonia and cramp-fasciculation syndrome with muscle twitching, cramps and stiffness.
Neuropathic pain, weight loss and profound sleep disruption are common and can dominate the clinical picture.
Thymoma is more frequently associated with CASPR2 antibodies than with LGI1, so tumour screening is particularly important, especially in Morvan syndrome.
Central features can include limbic encephalitis with memory impairment, seizures, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic instability.
Like LGI1, the antibody was historically grouped under the voltage-gated potassium channel complex; specific target confirmation is essential.
Older men are most often affected, and the disorder is frequently immunotherapy-responsive though recovery can be slow.
reference.pathophysiology: Contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2) is a transmembrane cell-adhesion molecule of the neurexin superfamily concentrated at the juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons and within central neurons, where together with contactin-2 (TAG-1) it anchors Kv1 voltage-gated potassium channels and maintains the segregation of ion channels essential for normal axonal conduction. Pathogenic IgG (with a substantial IgG4 component alongside IgG1) binds the discoidin and laminin-G-like domains of CASPR2, disrupting the CASPR2-contactin-2 interaction and destabilising juxtaparanodal potassium-channel clustering. Loss of this potassium-channel-mediated braking of excitability produces peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (neuromyotonia) and, centrally, limbic and autonomic network dysfunction. The wide anatomical distribution of CASPR2 explains the mixed central-peripheral phenotype and dysautonomia, while the IgG4 predominance again favours functional interference over destructive inflammation, correlating with potential reversibility. Thymic pathology and specific HLA associations implicate defective immune tolerance in initiating the response.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired neuromyotonia (Isaacs syndrome) of other cause
Motor neurone disease and other causes of fasciculation with cramp
Fatal familial insomnia and other prion disease
Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis with onconeural antibodies
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid cell-based assay for CASPR2 IgG
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography for neuromyotonic and fasciculation-cramp discharges
Brain MRI to assess medial temporal involvement
Cross-sectional chest imaging to screen for thymoma
Autonomic function testing where dysautonomia is prominent
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including oligoclonal bands and infection exclusion
Polysomnography or sleep assessment in suspected agrypnia excitata
redFlags: Morvan syndrome with severe insomnia, dysautonomia and encephalopathy requiring urgent evaluation
Autonomic instability with cardiac dysrhythmia or haemodynamic swings
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with continuous peripheral nerve hyperexcitability
Marked unexplained weight loss with severe neuropathic pain
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond well to immunotherapy and, where relevant, tumour treatment, though recovery may be gradual and dysautonomia can be life-threatening in Morvan syndrome. Prognosis is generally less favourable when a thymoma or malignancy is present.
pitfalls: Overlooking the peripheral nervous system and dysautonomia by focusing only on cognitive features
Failing to screen thoroughly for thymoma given its stronger association than with LGI1
Accepting a non-specific voltage-gated potassium channel positive result without CASPR2 target confirmation
Underestimating the danger of autonomic instability and severe insomnia in Morvan syndrome
Attributing neuromyotonia to a primary muscle disorder rather than an antibody-mediated cause
